content.overview: A laboratory result describes the submitted sample. Lot-level interpretation begins with a defensible lot definition and a sampling design that addresses meaningful heterogeneity.

vocabulary.definition: Material about which the sampling decision seeks to draw a conclusion.
Individual portion collected from a defined location or unit.
Combined increments prepared under a stated sampling design.

sections.title: Define the lot before collection
sections.body: Harvest identity, processing history, location, status and boundaries should be known before a sample is treated as representative.

sections.title: Address expected heterogeneity
sections.body: Container, rack, flower size, process zone and other meaningful sources of variation should inform selection rather than convenience.

sections.title: Preserve the sampling procedure
sections.body: Who collected, where, when, how much, with what tools and under which plan are part of the result context.

workedExamples: A top-of-bin grab sample is precise for that material but may not represent denser or differently exposed material elsewhere in the lot.
commonMistakes: Letting easy access define the sample.
Sampling before lot boundaries are resolved.
Calling a composite representative without documenting increments.
content.practicalApplication: Write a sampling map with lot definition, increments, locations, tools, sample amount, collector and rationale.
content.summary: Representative interpretation begins with a defined lot and a documented plan for its meaningful variation.
